Maladaptive Strategies.value: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy

Memory.value: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me

Negative Appraisals.value: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe
I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it

issues.explanation: The trigger set suggests a highly specific external threat context involving cyclists and thrown objects, but the rest of the profile (memory and appraisals) does not contain corresponding content about that kind of event. In a man-made disaster profile, 'burnt smell' coheres with disaster-related sensory memory, whereas 'people cycling' and 'throwing objects' pull toward a different trauma scenario and are hard to integrate with the remaining items.

'Avoid seeing friends' is not well supported by the rest of the selected profile. The active formulation strongly links Triggers with Memory and Maladaptive Strategies, and the endorsed strategies are otherwise cognitive/internal (thought avoidance, thought monitoring). Social avoidance could occur in PTSD, but here it is not tied to any endorsed trigger, memory content, or appraisal pattern, making it look like a strategy for a different symptom cluster than the one described.

vignette:
For 55-year-old David, a counselor in a community mental health clinic, the event that reshaped his life occurred during a group therapy session two years ago. A client, mid-rage, hurled a metal chair across the room. It struck a wall heater, which sparked and ignited a pile of papers. Smoke filled the room—thick, acrid, chemical—before David could wrestle the client to the ground and evacuate everyone. He remembers the sound of the chair, the heat, and most of all the smell: burnt plastic and insulation, a smell that still invades his present without warning.

In the weeks that followed, David struggled to make sense of his own reactions. He had always prided himself on being calm in a crisis, but now his body refused to cooperate. His heart would race at the whiff of a gas stove, or when a colleague tossed a jacket onto a chair. He came to believe that his body was betraying him—that it kept reacting as if he were still in that room, even when he was perfectly safe. This belief made him increasingly vigilant. He had to be especially careful, he told himself, because you never knew what could happen next. At work, he started scanning rooms for projectiles and exit routes before every session.

David’s memory of the event became strange to him. Sometimes, when he least expected it—while driving, or lying in bed—he would feel the full terror of that moment, the adrenaline spike, the helplessness, but without any clear image or memory attached. It was just the feeling, raw and disembodied. Other times, the memory would surface with a sensory clarity that felt unreal: he could smell the smoke and burnt plastic, and yet the entire scene felt as though it belonged to someone else, as if he were watching a movie about a stranger. He was certain that if he thought about the event deliberately, he would not be able to handle it, so he began monitoring his own thoughts constantly, searching for any sign that he was losing control. He avoided thinking about the therapy room entirely.

These strategies only deepened the memory’s alienation. The more he pushed the event away, the more it came back as a fragmented, intrusive sensation—the smell, the fear, the feeling that it wasn’t really his story. And each time that smell returned, it yanked him back into the past, reinforcing his belief that danger was always near. He started canceling plans with friends, telling himself he needed to stay home where it was safe. At the clinic, he asked to be reassigned to administrative duties, avoiding group rooms and the smell of burnt coffee from the break-room microwave.

The cycle tightened. A whiff of smoke from a neighbor’s barbecue would trigger a rush of fear, and David would spend the rest of the evening checking his own thoughts for signs of panic. The more he monitored, the more the alien, emotion-laden memory intruded. He had come to believe that his mind was untrustworthy, that thinking about the event would unravel him completely. His avoidance of friends left him isolated; his avoidance of thinking left him exhausted.

What finally brought David to seek help was a moment in the grocery store, when a customer dropped a glass jar near the deli counter. The sound—sharp, unexpected—sent him into a full panic attack in the cereal aisle. He stood there, shaking, smelling phantom smoke, feeling the terror of that room. He realized he could no longer manage this alone. What frightens him most now is the thought that his own mind is permanently broken, that he will never feel safe again. But beneath that, what he hopes for is simply to stop being a stranger to his own memory.
